hook: A gentleman burglar once stole a watch from Sherlock Holmes at the Château of Thibermesnil.

sections.voiceover: A gentleman burglar once stole a watch from Sherlock Holmes at the Château of Thibermesnil.
sections.visual_cue: Close-up of a Victorian-era pocket watch being lifted by gloved hands.
b_roll: Historical illustration of a 19th-century pocket watch

sections.voiceover: Arthur Conan Doyle introduced his famous London detective to the world in 1887. Does the London detective or the Paris gentleman burglar, Arsène Lupin, hold the superior edge?
sections.visual_cue: Split-screen showing London skyline on the left and Paris skyline on the right.

sections.voiceover: Brian Clark presented a 2024 comparative analysis to the John Openshaw Society in Houston, Texas.
sections.visual_cue: Document cover showing the John Openshaw Society logo.

sections.voiceover: David Drake from Université Paris VIII confirms Lupin solved the Château of Thibermesnil mystery. Lupin steals the watch while solving the mystery of the Château of Thibermesnil from Holmes.
sections.visual_cue: Diagram showing the Château of Thibermesnil location and a watch icon.
b_roll: Architectural sketch of a French chateau

sections.voiceover: Doyle published A Study in Scarlet in 1887, but Lupin ultimately secured the watch victory.
sections.visual_cue: Text overlay of the year 1887 fading into the name Arsène Lupin.
